claims.source_checked: Lobanov, Chicherov & Sharov 2021, doi:10.37482/issn2221-2698.2021.44.267: arcticandnorth.ru article pages (RU ELEMENT_ID=359546, EN ELEMENT_ID=360520) and both full-text PDFs (/upload/iblock/df4/267_284.pdf, /upload/iblock/61f/44_224_239.pdf, the journal's own English version, same DOI), read via pdftotext; doi:10.1038/s43247-026-03246-z: Crossref record read (title 'Ultradeep drilling beyond 10 km revealing new insights into Earth systems and resources', Commun. Earth Environ. 7:124, 3 Feb 2026, no abstract); www.nature.com article and PDF both 303-redirect to idp.nature.com, which the session network refuses (proxy 403 / ENOTFOUND). Full text NOT read.
claims.note: Lobanov 2021 (read): 'In 1990, the maximum depth was reached — 12262 m, which has not been surpassed so far'; 'This result has been unrivaled for 50 years'; 'the world's deepest scientific well, which reached a record depth of 12.262 m'. That confirms the record up to 2021. The claim is made in the present tense on 2026-11-18, and the SOURCES block rests the 2021-2026 part on Zhu & Huang 2026, which could not be opened. Change needed: read Zhu & Huang (allow idp.nature.com) and confirm it states SG-3 is still the deepest, or cite another A2 source dated after 2021. Note for pedants: Lobanov's figure is the depth of the deepest branch (the third shaft, 'started at a depth of 7010 m, ended at 12 262 m'); longer oil wells (measured length) are not covered by any source read, and the script rightly says 'deepest', not 'longest'.

claims.claim: ... was drilled with a bit narrower than a dinner plate.
claims.source_checked: Lobanov, Chicherov & Sharov 2021, doi:10.37482/issn2221-2698.2021.44.267: arcticandnorth.ru article pages (RU ELEMENT_ID=359546, EN ELEMENT_ID=360520) and both full-text PDFs (/upload/iblock/df4/267_284.pdf, /upload/iblock/61f/44_224_239.pdf, the journal's own English version, same DOI), read via pdftotext; Met Museum Collection API: v1.1/search?q=51.86.100 -> objectID 201074, v1/objects/201074
claims.note: Lobanov: 'a 46 m long multistage turbine at the bottom with a 214 mm drill bit'. Met 51.86.100 'Dinner plate', 'Diameter: 10 1/16 in. (25.6 cm)'; even the Met's smaller dinner plate 51.86.140 is 23.2 cm. 21.4 cm < 23-26 cm, so the wording holds. Popov's 214 mm open-hole figure was not read (see SOURCES items) but is not needed for this line.

claims.claim: A4 swipe-at-second-two reading: 'the deepest hole ever is about as narrow as a dinner plate'
claims.source_checked: Lobanov, Chicherov & Sharov 2021, doi:10.37482/issn2221-2698.2021.44.267: arcticandnorth.ru article pages (RU ELEMENT_ID=359546, EN ELEMENT_ID=360520) and both full-text PDFs (/upload/iblock/df4/267_284.pdf, /upload/iblock/61f/44_224_239.pdf, the journal's own English version, same DOI), read via pdftotext; USGS Open-File Report 86-517, https://pubs.usgs.gov/of/1986/0517/report.pdf (full PDF, pdftotext)
claims.note: The hook names the bit, which is true as stated. The impression a swiper may take, that the hole itself is that narrow, is true for most of its length but not everywhere: Lobanov, 'To a depth of about 7 km ... the borehole was flat, almost corresponding to the diameter of the drill bit', but below 7 km 'oval shape, many caverns appeared'; USGS OFR 86-517 p.(geophysics, neutron-gamma log) mentions readings 'where cavity diameter is greater than 40 cm', and the drilling chapter lists a 295.3 mm reamer. The script's choice to name the bit, not the hole, is what keeps the hook true; do not reword it to 'the hole is narrower than a dinner plate'. Also 'dug' for a drilled borehole is colloquial framing, corrected by 'drilled' in the same sentence. The whole hook still depends on claim 1 for 'deepest ever'.

claims.claim: And it never made it through the crust.

claims.claim: At the bottom, the rock was over two hundred degrees.
claims.source_checked: Lobanov, Chicherov & Sharov 2021, doi:10.37482/issn2221-2698.2021.44.267: arcticandnorth.ru article pages (RU ELEMENT_ID=359546, EN ELEMENT_ID=360520) and both full-text PDFs (/upload/iblock/df4/267_284.pdf, /upload/iblock/61f/44_224_239.pdf, the journal's own English version, same DOI), read via pdftotext
claims.note: Lobanov: 'the real temperature in the borehole at a depth of 10 km reached 180°С, and at a depth of about 12 km, the temperature values reached 212°С, instead of the assumed 120°С'. 212 °C at about 12 km = 'over two hundred'. The voice gives no unit; 212 °C is 414 °F, so the line is true whichever unit a viewer assumes. Lobanov says temperature 'in the borehole'; 'the rock' is a fair reading for a static bottom-hole measurement.

claims.claim: The hot rock kept closing the hole ...

Earth Environ. 7:124, 3 Feb 2026, no abstract); www.nature.com article and PDF both 303-redirect to idp.nature.com, which the session network refuses (proxy 403 / ENOTFOUND). Full text NOT read.
claims.note: Rests only on Zhu & Huang 2026 ('plastic rock flow that repeatedly sealed the hole'), which could not be opened. Lobanov 2021, which was read, does not attribute the hole's trouble to heat: 'less durable, fractured, interbedded Archean rocks ... went deeper than 7 km. Drilling became more difficult, and the borehole took on an oval shape, many caverns appeared, and accidents became more frequent'; 'in the Archean rocks, external influences led to collapse of the borehole walls and significant changes in its radial dimensions'. Caverns are the hole widening, not closing, so the read source gives a different mechanism. Change needed: either get Zhu & Huang read (allow idp.nature.com) and confirm the quoted sentence, or say what Lobanov supports, e.g. 'The rock kept caving in, and the money ran out.' (on screen 'CAVING ROCK' / 'FUNDING CUT'; post text 'the walls kept collapsing').
